230:
To acquiesce means to accept or go along with something without fighting it, even though you may not fully agree with it or like it.

It sits in a very specific emotional space: you're not happy about it, you're not enthusiastically agreeing — but you're also not resisting. You're simply choosing to let it happen. You are going along quietly.

Think of it as a silent nod when you'd rather say no.
What Makes It Different From Just "Agreeing"

This is the most important thing to understand. Acquiescing is not the same as agreeing.

When you agree with something, you genuinely think it's right or good. Your inside and outside match.

When you acquiesce, your inside and outside don't match. Inside, you may have doubts, discomfort, or even quiet opposition — but on the outside, you choose not to object. You let it pass. You go along.

This inner reluctance is the soul of the word. Without it, you'd just use "agree."

Imagine three people reacting to a decision they didn't ask for:

  • Person A says "Yes! Great idea! I love it!" → They agreed.
  • Person B says "Absolutely not. I refuse." → They resisted.
  • Person C says nothing. They sigh quietly, and go along with it, even though they're not thrilled. → They acquiesced.

Person C is acquiescing. They're not a fan, but they're not going to make a fight of it either.

Example 1 — Family life:
A teenager wants to stay out until midnight. The parents think 10 PM is better. After a long conversation, the parents eventually acquiesce — they allow midnight, even though they're still not fully comfortable with it. They didn't change their minds. They just stopped resisting.

Example 2 — The workplace:
In a team meeting, your manager proposes a plan you have reservations about. You raise a small concern, but the manager pushes forward. Rather than argue further, you acquiesce — you nod, stay quiet, and let it move ahead.

Example 3 — A big life decision:
A person's family strongly wants them to pursue a particular career. The person has other dreams, but over time, exhausted by the pressure, they acquiesce to the family's wishes. They follow the path without ever really wanting to.

In each case, notice: the person could have fought harder, but chose not to. That choice — to stop resisting — is what acquiescing is all about.

Acquiescing usually carries one or more of these feelings underneath it:

  • Resignation — "I've accepted this is how it's going to be."
  • Fatigue — "I'm too tired to keep fighting this."
  • Practicality — "It's not worth the conflict."
  • Pressure — "I felt I had no real choice."

This is why the word often appears in situations involving power imbalances, social pressure, or long negotiations. It suggests the person gave in, even without anyone forcing them.
How It's Used in a Sentence (Grammar)

Acquiesce is almost always followed by "to" or, in more formal writing, "in."

  • She acquiesced to her doctor's advice, even though she hated the idea of surgery.
  • The government acquiesced in the demands of the protesters.
  • He didn't want to move cities, but eventually acquiesced.
  • After hours of debate, the committee finally acquiesced.

Both "acquiesce to" and "acquiesce in" are correct. "Acquiesce to" is more natural in everyday modern English. "Acquiesce in" sounds more formal or old-fashioned.

• Acquiescence (noun) — the act of acquiescing. "Her acquiescence surprised everyone who expected a fight."
  • Acquiescent (adjective) — describing a person or attitude that tends to go along without resisting. "He was too acquiescent — he never stood up for himself."

To sharpen the word further, here's what it should not be confused with:

  • Approve — to approve is to think something is good. Acquiescing carries no such positive judgment.
  • Surrender — surrender implies defeat in a conflict. Acquiescing is softer; you simply stop objecting.
  • Obey — obeying is following a command. Acquiescing has no explicit command — you choose to go along.
  • Pretend to agree — acquiescing isn't deceitful. You're not pretending to agree. You're genuinely choosing not to oppose, while still holding your own quiet feelings.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

To acquiesce = to stop resisting and go along with something, quietly and without protest, even though part of you doesn't want to.

Whenever you see this word, picture someone who had doubts, had maybe even pushed back a little — and then, in the end, let out a quiet breath and said, in effect: "Fine. Alright. We'll do it your way." That is acquiescing.
231:
Acquiescence is the act of quietly going along with something — accepting it, allowing it, or letting it happen — without openly agreeing to it, but also without resisting or objecting to it.

It sits in an interesting middle ground: you're not saying "yes, I love this idea" — but you're also not saying "no, I refuse." You simply... don't push back. You let it pass. That silence or passivity is the acquiescence.

Think of it this way: imagine your friends are deciding where to eat, and they pick a place you're not excited about. You don't protest. You just shrug and go along. That shrug — that quiet, non-resistant acceptance — is acquiescence.
The Key Quality: It Is Passive

The most important thing to understand about acquiescence is that it is passive by nature. It is consent given through inaction or silence, not through enthusiastic agreement.

  • Active agreement: "Yes! Great idea, I'm in!"
  • Acquiescence: "...okay, fine." (or even just silence)
  • Refusal: "No, I don't want this."

You can acquiesce without even saying a single word. By simply not objecting — by letting something happen — you have acquiesced to it.

Acquiescence almost always carries a quiet undercurrent of reluctance, resignation, or mild discomfort. The person acquiescing often has reservations, doubts, or even disagreements — but they have chosen not to voice or act on them.

Why might someone acquiesce?

  • They feel that objecting is pointless or won't change anything.
  • They want to avoid conflict or confrontation.
  • They feel pressured, even if no one is explicitly forcing them.
  • They are tired of fighting the same battle.
  • They simply don't care enough to resist.
  • They feel the other person or authority holds more power.

This is what separates acquiescence from genuine, wholehearted agreement. When you truly agree with something, there is no holding back. With acquiescence, there is something being held back — and the person just decides not to act on it.

Acquiescence describes both a single act and an ongoing attitude or pattern.

As a single act:

After arguing for weeks, he finally showed his acquiescence by nodding and saying nothing more.

As an ongoing attitude:

The people's acquiescence to the new rules surprised many activists — they had expected protests.

It is frequently used to describe:

  • A person going along with someone else's decision or wish
  • A group or population that does not resist authority
  • Someone giving in during a negotiation or argument
  • A child who stops fighting a parent's rule
  • A legal or contractual situation where one party's silence is taken as acceptance
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise:

Agreement — You are on board. You genuinely support or approve of something. There is no reluctance. Acquiescence lacks this genuine buy-in.

Consent — You are actively giving permission. You communicate it. Acquiescence is more passive — it can happen through mere silence or inaction.

Submission — You are giving in to a stronger force, often under pressure or coercion. It suggests defeat. Acquiescence is quieter and less dramatic — there is no sense of being overpowered, just a personal choice not to resist.

Compliance — You are following rules or instructions, usually because you have to. Acquiescence is more about choosing not to object than about following something.

Reluctant acceptance — This is the closest plain-English equivalent to acquiescence. But acquiescence is the single, precise, formal word for it.

Acquiescence can be:

Genuine and unbothered: Sometimes people acquiesce because the matter simply isn't important enough to fight over. A friend picks a movie you're neutral about — you acquiesce without any real inner conflict.

Resigned and weary: The person is unhappy but has decided that fighting is not worth it anymore. This is the most emotionally heavy form.

Calculated or strategic: A person deliberately stays silent — perhaps to keep peace, or because they plan to address the matter later, or because they want to appear cooperative.

Coerced or fearful: The person feels they have no real choice. Even if no one is forcing them openly, they acquiesce because the cost of refusing feels too high. This is one of the most ethically important uses of the word — acquiescence under such conditions is not truly free consent.

1. Her silence was taken as acquiescence — no one realized she was deeply uncomfortable with the decision.
  2. The board's acquiescence to the CEO's demands shocked the shareholders.
  3. Through years of acquiescence, he had let others make every major decision in his life.
  4. The new law passed largely because of public acquiescence — people grumbled but did not protest.
  5. She smiled, but her acquiescence was clear in her slumped shoulders.

Acquiescence is ultimately about the choice not to resist. It is acceptance that is quiet, passive, and often tinged with reservation. It is important to understand because it describes a very real and very common human experience — the experience of going along with something not because you love it, but because you have decided, for whatever reason, that you will not fight it.

When you understand acquiescence, you also start to understand a deeper idea: that silence is not always neutrality. Sometimes, silence is itself a kind of answer.
232:
Acquiescent describes a person who accepts, agrees with, or goes along with something — without arguing, resisting, or pushing back — even when they may not be fully happy about it.

Think of it as a quiet "okay." Not a excited "yes!", not an angry "no!" — just a passive, uncomplaining acceptance.
The Key Idea: Acceptance Without Resistance

The heart of this word is not fighting back. An acquiescent person doesn't protest, doesn't object, and doesn't try to change the situation. They simply... go along with it.

Imagine your boss at work gives you extra tasks that you weren't expecting and don't particularly want. You might grumble privately inside your head, but outwardly, you just nod and say "Sure." That's being acquiescent — you accepted the situation without resistance, even though it wasn't what you wanted.
What Makes It Different from Simply "Agreeing"

This is a very important distinction. Agreeing means you actually think something is right, fair, or good. Acquiescent doesn't require that. You can be acquiescent even when you disagree internally — you just choose not to challenge it or make a fuss.

In other words:

  • Agreeing = "I think this is right."
  • Acquiescent = "I'm not going to fight this, even if I'm not thrilled about it."

An acquiescent person may have their own thoughts and feelings, but they suppress them and comply anyway. The compliance is the outward behavior; what's happening inside may be a completely different story.
The Emotional Tone: Passive, Not Enthusiastic

Acquiescent carries a feeling of passivity and submission. It's not energetic. It's not joyful. It's quiet compliance. You'd never describe someone who is cheering, enthusiastically involved, or genuinely on board with something as acquiescent. The word only fits when there's that element of going along rather than driving forward.

Think of the difference between a child who wants to eat their vegetables (agreeable, enthusiastic) vs. one who silently eats them because they've learned that fighting it is pointless (acquiescent). The second child isn't happy about it — but they're not fighting it either.

Acquiescent is not a neutral word. It usually carries a mildly critical or unflattering tone, especially when used to describe a person or behavior. It suggests weakness, lack of assertiveness, or an unwillingness to stand up for oneself or what is right.

Calling someone acquiescent often implies they are:

  • Too easy to push around
  • Lacking the backbone to resist authority or pressure
  • Willing to tolerate things they shouldn't
  • More concerned with keeping the peace than with justice or truth

For example: "The committee was acquiescent in the face of the CEO's bad decisions" — this suggests the committee should have pushed back, but didn't.

That said, the word is not always harshly negative. In some contexts, being acquiescent can be viewed as cooperative, humble, or even wise — particularly when resisting something would be pointless, dangerous, or socially disruptive. But even then, a slight sense of excessive submission tends to linger.

Acquiescence isn't all-or-nothing. Think of it as sitting on a spectrum:

Total resistance → Reluctant compliance → Acquiescence → Willingness → Enthusiasm

Acquiescent sits in that quietly compliant middle zone. The person isn't digging their heels in, but they're not happy volunteers either. They've essentially decided that going along is easier than resisting — or that they have no real choice.
Who or What Can Be Acquiescent?

The adjective can describe:

  • A person: "She was an acquiescent student who never questioned the teacher's decisions, even when they were unfair."
  • A group or institution: "The board was acquiescent, letting the chairman do whatever he wished without challenge."
  • A person's behavior or manner: "He gave an acquiescent nod when asked to work overtime."
  • A response or attitude: "Her acquiescent silence was mistaken for agreement."

These will help you feel the word in action:

  1. "The employees were so acquiescent that the manager had no idea they were deeply unhappy — nobody ever spoke up."

(The employees kept accepting things quietly without complaint.)

  1. "He was tired of being acquiescent in a relationship where his opinions were constantly dismissed."

(He had been going along with things too much, without pushing back.)

  1. "The country's parliament was acquiescent, rubber-stamping every law the president proposed without debate."

(The parliament offered no resistance or scrutiny — just approval.)

  1. "She answered in an acquiescent tone, though her eyes revealed she disagreed completely."

(Her words and behavior showed acceptance, but internally she didn't agree.)

  1. "Raising acquiescent children who never question anything is not the same as raising respectful children."

(Children who blindly comply are different from children who consciously choose respectful behavior.)
The Subtle but Important Distinction from Related Words

• Obedient — Following rules or commands, often out of respect or duty. Obedience can be positive and principled. Acquiescent is more passive and often suggests a lack of will.
  • Submissive — Similar, but stronger. Submissive implies a deeper, possibly chronic yielding to others, often to a troubling degree. Acquiescent is slightly softer.
  • Compliant — More neutral. Compliant simply means you follow instructions or rules. It doesn't carry the same implication of inner reluctance or passivity as acquiescent.
  • Resigned — Means you've accepted something unpleasant as inevitable, often with sadness. Acquiescent focuses on the lack of resistance; resigned focuses on the emotional acceptance of something unwanted.

If you need to remember just one thing: Acquiescent means quietly going along with something without complaint or resistance — not because you necessarily agree or are happy — but because you choose not to fight it.
233:
To acquire something means to come to have something that you did not have before — through some kind of process, effort, or experience.

That process could be buying it, learning it, practicing it, or simply experiencing something repeatedly over time until it becomes yours.

You could say "I got a new skill" or "I acquired a new skill" — both are correct. But "acquire" carries a slightly richer meaning.

When you use "acquire," it quietly suggests:

  • A process was involved — it didn't just fall into your lap.
  • You now genuinely possess it — it has become truly yours.
  • It often took some effort, time, or experience to get there.

"Acquire" is also slightly more formal and precise than "get," which is why you'll see it more in professional, academic, and business writing.
The Two Broad Ways Something Is Acquired

1. You actively pursue and obtain it

Here, you deliberately go after something and make it yours. This can be through:

  • Buying or purchasing: "The company acquired land near the river to build a new factory."
  • Formal or legal means: "She acquired ownership of the property after her aunt passed away."
  • Taking over another business: In the business world, "acquire" very commonly means one company buys and takes over another. "The tech giant acquired a smaller startup for two billion dollars."

2. It develops in you gradually, through experience

Here, you don't make one clear decision to "get" it — it builds up slowly as a result of repeated exposure, practice, or experience. This is where "acquire" is especially useful:

  • Skills and abilities: "He acquired fluency in Japanese after living in Tokyo for three years."
  • Knowledge: "Over decades of reading, she acquired a vast knowledge of history."
  • Habits: "He had acquired the habit of waking up before sunrise."
  • Tastes and preferences: "I never liked black coffee as a child, but I acquired a taste for it in college."

That last phrase — "acquire a taste" — is very common in English. It means you grew to enjoy something you didn't like or understand at first, after repeated exposure.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Acquired?

"Acquire" is a flexible word. You can acquire:

CategoryExample
Physical objects or propertyland, a house, a painting
Money or wealthfunds, assets
Skillsa language, a craft, coding
Knowledgeinformation, expertise, wisdom
Qualities and traitsconfidence, patience, discipline
Habitsa routine, a bad habit, a good habit
A taste or likinga taste for jazz, spicy food, literature
Companies or assets (in business)a startup, a brand, a patent

"Acquire" always carries the feeling that something has moved from "not yours" to "yours" — whether that thing is an object sitting in a room, a skill sitting in your mind, or a habit woven into your daily life.

It does not matter whether the process was quick (signing a purchase agreement) or slow (developing patience over years). What matters is: at some point, you didn't have it — and now you do, and it belongs to you in a real sense.

• Acquire is always a transitive verb — meaning it must be followed by an object. You always acquire something. You cannot just say "She acquired" without saying what.
  • Past tense: acquired
  • Present participle: acquiring
  • Noun form: acquisition ("The acquisition of new skills takes time.")
  • The person doing the acquiring: acquirer (common in business — the company doing the buying)

• "Children acquire language naturally by listening and speaking."
  • "The museum acquired three rare paintings from a private collector."
  • "Through years of practice, he acquired the precision of a master craftsman."
  • "She slowly acquired the confidence to speak in front of large audiences."
  • "The government acquired the building to convert it into a public library."
  • "It's an acquired taste — most people don't enjoy it immediately."
To acquire something means to come to genuinely possess something — whether an object, skill, quality, or habit — through a process of purchase, effort, practice, or gradual experience.
234:
When "acquired" describes something, it means that thing was not there from the start — it came later, through experience, exposure, learning, or some kind of process. It wasn't natural, inborn, or original. It was gained over time.

The clearest way to understand it is through its opposite. The opposite of acquired is innate — meaning something you were born with, something natural and original. If something is innate, it was always there. If something is acquired, it arrived through life.
The most important usage: "An acquired taste"

This is the phrase you'll encounter most often, and it captures the word's spirit perfectly.

An acquired taste is something you didn't enjoy — or even disliked — the first time you encountered it, but gradually came to appreciate or enjoy after repeated exposure. The liking had to be developed. It wasn't immediate or natural.

"Black coffee is an acquired taste."
"He says jazz was an acquired taste for him — he couldn't stand it at first."
"Sushi is often described as an acquired taste by people who didn't grow up eating it."

The phrase carries a gentle, important message: don't dismiss something just because you don't like it right away. With time and exposure, you might grow to love it. The taste has to be earned, cultivated, built up — it doesn't come for free.

This phrase also works beyond food. You might describe a person's dry sense of humor, a challenging author's writing style, or even a difficult piece of classical music as an acquired taste.

Acquired skills and knowledge
Any ability, language, or knowledge you learned and developed through effort — not a talent you were born with — is acquired.

"Her fluency in French is entirely acquired — she began studying at age twenty."
"Programming is an acquired skill. Nobody is born knowing how to code."

Acquired immunity (medicine)
Your body has two kinds of immunity: the kind you're born with (innate immunity), and the kind your body builds up after fighting off a disease or receiving a vaccine. The second type is acquired immunity — your system learned to defend itself through experience.

"The vaccine gives you acquired immunity against the virus."

Acquired characteristics (biology)
Traits or features a living thing develops during its lifetime due to its environment, behavior, or experiences — as opposed to traits it inherited genetically from its parents.

"The thick calluses on his hands are acquired characteristics from years of physical labor."

Acquired habits, wealth, or status
Habits you developed over time, wealth you built through work, or social standing you earned — not something you were born into — can all be described as acquired.

"His love of discipline is an acquired habit, shaped by years in the military."
"Her acquired wealth stood in contrast to those who had inherited theirs."
The quiet implication of the word

"Acquired" doesn't simply mean "gotten" or "obtained." It carries a richer suggestion: that some process was involved — time, effort, exposure, or experience. Something acquired wasn't handed to you instantly. It came through living, learning, or being shaped by the world.

It also subtly implies that the thing wasn't obvious or natural at first. It had to be grown into. This is exactly why it works so powerfully in the phrase "acquired taste" — the appreciation had to be cultivated, not assumed.
How to recognize it in any new context

Whenever you see "acquired" as an adjective and aren't sure what it means in that moment, ask yourself one simple question:

"Was this always there — or did it come through some kind of process?"

If it came through a process of gaining, developing, or building over time, it's acquired. If it was there from the very beginning, naturally and originally, it's not.

That one question will serve you in every context you ever meet this word.
235:
When something is called "an acquired taste," it means something that most people do not like the first time they experience it, but can gradually come to enjoy after repeated exposure over time.

The key idea here is simple: the liking was not natural or instant — it was developed. You were not born appreciating it. You acquired (= slowly gained or developed) the ability to enjoy it.

The phrase is rooted in the literal act of tasting food or drink. Think about coffee, for example. The first time most people taste black coffee, they find it bitter and unpleasant. But after drinking it many times, they begin to enjoy — and even crave — that very same bitterness. The taste was not always there; it was acquired through repeated experience.

Other classic food examples include:

  • Blue cheese (very strong and pungent)
  • Oysters (strange texture and oceanic flavour)
  • Dark chocolate (intensely bitter)
  • Olives (salty and sharp)
  • Beer (bitter and yeasty to first-time drinkers)

These things share a common thread: they are complex, strong, or unusual, and they reward patience and familiarity rather than giving instant pleasure.

The word "acquired" simply means obtained or developed gradually over time. It is the opposite of something that is natural, instant, or inborn.

So when you put it together:

Acquired + Taste = A liking that was developed over time, not felt immediately.
Beyond Food — The Figurative (and More Common) Use

While the phrase was born from literal tasting, today it is used much more broadly to describe almost anything — music, art, films, humor, fashion, literature, hobbies, and even people's personalities.

Examples in sentences:

  • "Jazz music is an acquired taste — many people find it confusing at first, but they eventually fall in love with it."
  • "His dry, deadpan humor is an acquired taste; some people find him hilarious, while others don't get it at first."
  • "Abstract art is often an acquired taste — it takes time to understand what the artist is expressing."
  • "She's a bit of an acquired taste as a person — blunt and intense, but once you know her, she's wonderful."
  • "I've developed an acquired taste for very spicy food after living in India for a year."

Calling someone "an acquired taste" means they have a strong, unusual, or unconventional personality that not everyone warms up to immediately. It means people may need time and repeated interaction before they truly appreciate and like that person.

This is not an insult. It is more of a candid, affectionate observation — suggesting the person has depth or character that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once.
The Tone: Is It Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

The idiom is generally neutral to mildly positive. Here is how to think about it:

  • It does not mean something is bad or of low quality.
  • It does not mean everyone will eventually like it.
  • It does mean the thing has a certain depth, complexity, or unusualness that takes time to appreciate.
  • It often carries a subtle suggestion of sophistication — implying that people who do enjoy it have developed a more refined or open-minded sense of appreciation.

Think of it this way: saying "wine is an acquired taste" is very different from saying "wine tastes terrible." The first is respectful and observational; the second is a flat-out rejection.

The tone can shift slightly depending on context and delivery:

  • Said with warmth → it is a compliment wrapped in honesty.
  • Said with a slight sigh → it can be a polite way of saying "most people won't enjoy this."

But in almost all cases, it is never a harsh criticism.

1. It implies real value exists.
Calling something an acquired taste suggests it is worth persisting with. You would not typically call something truly awful an acquired taste — that would just be called "bad." The phrase implies there is something genuinely worthwhile underneath the initial strangeness.

2. The initial dislike is not permanent.
The whole point of the phrase is that first impressions are not final. With time and familiarity, appreciation can grow.

3. Not everyone will acquire the taste.
The phrase does not promise that everyone will eventually like it. It simply means some people come to love it after repeated exposure. Others may never warm up to it, and that is perfectly normal too.

4. Exposure is the key ingredient.
The "acquiring" happens through repeated, willing exposure. You try something multiple times, in different settings, with an open mind — and over time, what once felt strange starts to feel familiar, then enjoyable.

The most common structures are:

  • "[Something] is an acquired taste." → General statement.
  • "[Someone/Something] is a bit of an acquired taste." → Softened, conversational version.
  • "I've developed an acquired taste for [something]." → Talking about yourself.
  • "[Something] can be an acquired taste for many people." → Acknowledging variation between people.

The beauty of this idiom is that it reflects a very human truth: not everything worthwhile is immediately obvious. Some of the finest things in life — whether a genre of music, a type of food, a style of humour, or a remarkable person — ask you to slow down, be patient, and give them a fair chance. An acquired taste is life's gentle reminder that first impressions are not always the whole story.
236:
Acquisition means the act of getting something, or the thing that was gotten. That's the simplest way to put it. But to truly understand this word, you need to see both of those meanings clearly, because the word flips between them depending on how it's used.

When someone says "the acquisition of new skills takes time," the word refers to the process — the act of gaining those skills. When someone says "this painting is my finest acquisition," the word refers to the thing itself — the painting they obtained. One word, two closely related meanings, and context tells you which one is meant.
What Makes Something an "Acquisition" and Not Just "Getting"?

This is a subtle but important distinction. You get a cold by accident. You get bored without trying. But an acquisition almost always involves deliberate effort, intention, or transaction. It implies that something of value was sought out and obtained — whether that's through purchase, effort, strategy, or formal process.

This is why "acquisition" sounds formal and purposeful. It carries weight. You wouldn't casually say "I made an acquisition at the grocery store." But you absolutely would say "the museum's latest acquisition is a rare 16th-century manuscript," because that suggests deliberate pursuit, selection, and obtaining of something significant.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

1. The World of Business and Organizations

This is where the word is most powerful and most commonly heard in the news. When one company buys another company — fully takes it over — that is called an acquisition. The buying company absorbs the other: its employees, its products, its assets, its brand, everything.

For example, if a large tech company purchases a small startup, the news will report it as "Company A completes acquisition of Company B." The word here captures the entire event — the negotiation, the deal, the transfer of ownership — in a single, precise term.

An important concept linked to this is a hostile acquisition (sometimes called a hostile takeover). This is when one company forcibly acquires another against the wishes of the target company's management. It's called "hostile" because the target company resists, but the acquiring company pushes through anyway, often by buying enough shares to take control.

2. The World of Learning, Skills, and Knowledge

"Acquisition" is widely used to describe how people gain non-physical things like knowledge, skills, habits, and language. The phrase language acquisition, for example, is a major field of study in linguistics and psychology. It refers to how human beings — especially children — naturally absorb and learn to use a language.

You'll also hear phrases like "the acquisition of expertise," "the acquisition of critical thinking skills," or "knowledge acquisition." In all these cases, the word dignifies the process — it signals that gaining this thing required real effort, time, or immersion.

Outside business and learning, "acquisition" is used more loosely but still purposefully.

In museums, libraries, and art galleries, new acquisitions are new items added to a collection. A museum might announce "our recent acquisitions include three paintings from the Dutch Golden Age." This is the formal vocabulary of institutions building their collections over time.

In personal life, someone might refer to a prized new purchase as an acquisition — particularly when it's something they researched, saved up for, or hunted down. A collector showing off a rare vinyl record might say, "This is my most exciting acquisition this year." The word signals that it wasn't random — it was sought.

In military and geopolitical contexts, acquisition refers to gaining territory, resources, or assets, often through force or negotiation. "The acquisition of new territory" is the kind of phrase you'd read in a history book about empires expanding.

In technology and data, you'll hear "data acquisition" — the process of collecting and recording data from sensors, systems, or environments. It's a very technical usage, but the core idea is the same: deliberately gathering something of value.
The Two Grammar Shapes of the Word

Understanding how the word behaves grammatically will help you use it correctly.

When "acquisition" is uncountable, it refers to the general process or act of obtaining: "Acquisition of wealth was his lifelong pursuit." No article, no plural — just the idea itself.

When "acquisition" is countable, it refers to a specific thing that was obtained: "The company announced three major acquisitions this quarter." Here it's being treated like a concrete object you can count.

Both are correct — which form you use depends on whether you're talking about the process or the result.
How It Typically Pairs With Other Words

Certain words naturally sit beside "acquisition" in real usage. Knowing these pairings will make the word feel natural to you:

You make an acquisition. You don't "do" one or "take" one. Companies make acquisitions. Collectors make acquisitions.

Acquisitions are described as recent, major, latest, key, strategic, hostile, or prized — all of these tell you something about the nature or importance of what was obtained.

You speak of the acquisition of something: the acquisition of land, the acquisition of a competitor, the acquisition of fluency, the acquisition of taste.
The Single Sentence That Holds It All Together

If you had to carry one sentence in your mind to anchor this word forever, let it be this:

An acquisition is something valuable that was deliberately obtained — or the deliberate act of obtaining it — whether that something is a company, a skill, an object, knowledge, or territory.

Every use of the word, in every context, is a variation of that idea.
237:
Acquisitive describes a person (or group) who has a strong, constant desire to get and keep things — especially money, possessions, or power. Think of someone who always wants more, who is always reaching out to grab and hold onto things. That person is acquisitive.

The key idea is not just wanting something. Everybody wants things. What makes someone acquisitive is that the desire to accumulate — to pile things up, to own more and more — feels almost like a drive they can't turn off.

Acquisitive usually carries a slightly negative tone. It quietly suggests that the person's desire to acquire things has gone beyond normal or healthy. It hints at greediness, at a kind of restless hunger that is never quite satisfied. It is a more polished and formal word than "greedy," but it points in the same direction.

When you call someone acquisitive, you are not just saying they like nice things. You are saying that getting and owning things is a defining feature of how they live and what they want from life.

Most often, acquisitive refers to the desire for material things: money, property, land, objects, luxury goods, businesses. But the word is flexible enough to stretch beyond the material world:

  • A person can be acquisitive about power — always seeking more influence or control.
  • A person can be acquisitive about knowledge — always hungry to learn and collect information. In this case, the word actually loses most of its negative feeling and can even sound like a compliment.
  • A company can be acquisitive if it keeps buying up other companies and absorbing them.

So the heart of the word is the accumulating impulse — the urge to keep gathering, regardless of what is being gathered.

• "He was so acquisitive that even after buying his fifth car, he was already browsing ads for a sixth."
  • "The acquisitive businesswoman bought up every empty plot of land in the neighborhood, one by one."
  • "Growing up poor had made him quietly acquisitive — he found it deeply uncomfortable not to have savings."
  • "She had an acquisitive mind, absorbing every book, documentary, and conversation she could find on the subject."
  • "The company's acquisitive strategy left it owning dozens of brands across three continents."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close neighbors of acquisitive, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Greedy is the most everyday word. It is blunt and strong. You call a child greedy for grabbing all the cookies. You call a villain greedy. It is also often about food or money specifically.

Avaricious is almost exclusively about money and wealth. It is more intense and literary — it sounds more like a character flaw than a personality trait.

Covetous specifically means wanting what other people have. It is rooted in envy. An acquisitive person wants more in general; a covetous person wants yours specifically.

Materialistic describes someone who values physical possessions above other things in life, like relationships or experiences. It is about priorities and values.

Acquisitive is the most neutral of this group and the most versatile. It focuses on the act of accumulating — the habit or drive of always wanting to acquire — more than on the moral judgment of it. It is also the most comfortable word to use in formal or professional writing.

One important thing to understand: the word implies excess. Saving money, collecting books, buying a home — these are normal things. Nobody calls you acquisitive for that. The word kicks in when the desire to acquire has become notably strong, persistent, or defining. It is a word about degree.

Rarely, but yes. When applied to the mind or to learning, acquisitive can feel admiring: an acquisitive intellect is a compliment — it means a sharp, hungry, curious mind that absorbs everything. Outside of that, the word is mostly neutral-to-negative in tone.

From the same root, you get:

  • Acquisitiveness (noun) — the quality or state of being acquisitive. "Her acquisitiveness made her wealthy but lonely."
  • Acquisitively (adverb) — in an acquisitive manner. "He eyed the antique shop acquisitively."
  • Acquisition (noun) — the thing acquired, or the act of acquiring. "The museum announced its latest acquisition."
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: acquisitive = always wanting to get more and keep it, with a quiet suggestion that this desire has become excessive.
238:
Acquisitiveness is the strong, persistent desire to get and own things — whether money, objects, power, knowledge, or anything else of value.

It is the quality of always wanting to acquire (gain or collect) more. A person with acquisitiveness is never truly satisfied with what they already have; there is always a pull toward getting more.

Think of it this way: imagine someone who already has a comfortable home, a good salary, and more clothes than they can wear — yet they constantly shop, hoard, and scheme to get more wealth or possessions. That restless, driven hunger to keep accumulating is acquisitiveness. It is not just a single act of buying or collecting. It is a character trait — a deep, ongoing tendency in a person's personality.

Mostly, yes — the word carries a negative connotation. It suggests a kind of greediness or self-serving materialism. When someone is described as "full of acquisitiveness," the implication is that they are overly focused on personal gain, often at the expense of other values like generosity, contentment, or integrity.

However, in rare, neutral contexts, it can simply mean a strong drive to acquire things — for example, a scholar's acquisitiveness for knowledge. Here, the word doesn't judge; it just describes the intensity of the desire. But even in such cases, the word hints at an excessive quality.
How it differs from related ideas

• Greed is the intense craving for something (often wealth), focused on the feeling of wanting. Acquisitiveness is slightly broader — it is the behavioral tendency to actually go out and collect or obtain things. Greed is the fire inside; acquisitiveness is the fire expressed as action and habit.
  • Materialism is the belief that owning things is what makes life valuable. Acquisitiveness is the active drive that often fuels materialism — the engine behind it.
  • Ambition is the desire to achieve something meaningful (a goal, a position, success). Acquisitiveness is narrower and more self-serving — it is about accumulating for yourself, not necessarily about achievement.

• "His acquisitiveness was so extreme that even after becoming a billionaire, he continued to cut corners and underpay his workers to grow his fortune."
  • "The collector's acquisitiveness led her to fill three warehouses with art, most of which she never even looked at."
  • "Politicians driven by acquisitiveness tend to abuse their positions for personal financial gain."
  • "There is a difference between healthy ambition and hollow acquisitiveness — one builds something meaningful, the other just hoards."

If you had to reduce acquisitiveness to one sentence:

It is the habitual, often insatiable urge to keep acquiring and possessing more — money, things, or influence — beyond what is reasonably needed, and it usually reflects a self-absorbed or greedy aspect of a person's character.

It describes not a single moment of wanting something, but a lasting disposition — a consistent pattern of who someone is, not just what they do once.
239: "Acquit" is a verb with two distinct meanings. Both are important, and both are used in modern English.
Meaning 1: To officially declare someone not guilty

This is the most common meaning of the word, and it lives almost entirely in the world of law and justice.

When a person is accused of a crime and put on trial, a judge or jury carefully examines all the evidence. At the end, they deliver a verdict — a decision. That decision is either guilty or not guilty. If they decide the person did not commit the crime, they acquit that person.

Think of it this way: to acquit someone is to officially clear their name.

The jury acquitted him after three days of deliberation.
She was acquitted of all charges.
The court acquitted the man due to lack of evidence.

A few things to note about this meaning:

  • The person who does the acquitting is always an authority — a jury, a judge, or a court. A friend cannot "acquit" you. Your boss cannot "acquit" you. Only a legal body can.
  • The person being acquitted is always the accused — someone who was formally charged with a crime.
  • When someone is acquitted, it doesn't always mean the world believes they are innocent. It means the legal system, by its rules and standards, did not find enough proof to declare them guilty. These two things — legal acquittal and moral innocence — can sometimes be different, and people often debate this.
  • The noun form of this word is acquittal (the act or result of being acquitted). "The acquittal shocked the public."
  • The direct opposite of acquit is convict — to officially find someone guilty.
Meaning 2: To acquit oneself — to perform or conduct oneself in a certain way

This is a completely different meaning, and it has nothing to do with crime or courts. Here, "acquit" is always used in the reflexive form — meaning it is always paired with a reflexive pronoun: acquit himself, acquit herself, acquit themselves, acquit yourself, acquit myself.

When you say someone "acquitted themselves" in a situation, you are describing how well or how poorly they handled themselves — how they performed, behaved, or came across — especially in a challenging, important, or high-pressure situation.

She acquitted herself brilliantly in the job interview. (= She performed very well.)
Despite being nervous, the young soldier acquitted himself with courage. (= He conducted himself bravely.)
The new teacher acquitted herself poorly on her first day. (= She didn't do well.)
The team acquitted themselves honorably in defeat. (= They behaved with dignity even though they lost.)

Notice that this meaning almost always comes with a word that tells you how the person acquitted themselves — words like well, badly, honorably, brilliantly, poorly, admirably. Without such a word, the sentence feels incomplete.

This meaning is somewhat formal and literary in tone. You're more likely to see it in writing, journalism, literature, or formal speech than in casual everyday conversation. If you said to a friend, "You really acquitted yourself well today!" it would sound a little formal but perfectly correct and impressive.

At first glance, these two meanings seem completely unrelated — one is about courtrooms, the other is about personal performance. But there is a thread connecting them. In both cases, the word carries the sense of coming through a test or challenge and being judged — either by a court or by the standards of a situation. In the legal sense, the court judges you and clears you. In the personal sense, a situation tests you and you come through it (well or poorly). The word carries a quiet sense of proving oneself.

• To acquit someone = for a court or jury to officially declare that person not guilty of a crime.
  • To acquit oneself = to perform, behave, or conduct oneself in a particular way when facing a challenge or test.

Master these two uses and you have fully understood this word.
